input: Given question: What does it mean by isovolumetric contraction of the heart? Option A: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers but there is a decrease in volume. Option B: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers and the volume does not decrease. Option C: This is when the atrium contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the atrioventricular valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. Option D: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.05s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are open and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is no shortening of muscle fibers but emptying happens. Option E: This is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. The correct answer is Option E.
reference: Answer = E - Isovolumetric contractionThis is when the ventricles contracts for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. Atrial contraction (options A & B) refers to the initial phase of ventricular contraction where the atria contract first before the ventricles. However, atrial contraction is part of ventricular systole and is not a separate phase. Semilunar valve opening and closing (options C & D) occurs during ventricular diastole, not systole. During ventricular systole, the semilunar valves are closed. During ventricular diastole, the semilunar valves open, allowing blood to flow back into the atria. best_explanation: Answer E is correct. During isovolumetric contraction, the ventricles contract for the first 0.02-0.03s which is the time taken to build up pressure. During this period, the semilunar valves are closed and even though contraction occurs in ventricles, there is little shortening of muscle fibers and there is no emptying. After this period, the atrioventricular valves open and the ventricles continue to contract to empty their contents. This is one of the 3 phases of ventricular contraction. The other 2 are ventricular ejection and passive filling. input: Given question: In the production of prostaglandins, the most widely used fatty acid precursor called arachidonic acid must be made. For this to happen, the fatty acid must be cleaved from the membrane phospholipids through the action of an enzyme.What is the name of this enzyme? Option A: Phospholipase B2 - PLB2 Option B: Phospholipase B1 - PLB1 Option C: Phospholipase C Option D: Phospholipase A2 - PLA2 Option E: Phospholipase A1 - PLA1 The correct answer is Option D.
reference: A = incorrect - PLB2 is an enzyme involved in the breakdown of membrane phospholipids of the neuron, to release unsaturated fatty acids, mainly AA, for the synthesis of prostaglandins, and other eicosanoids. B = incorrect - PLB1 is an enzyme involved in the breakdown of membrane phospholipids of the neuron, to release unsaturated fatty acids, mainly AA, for the synthesis of prostaglandins, and other eicosanoids. C = incorrect - Phospholipase C is a general term for two different but related enzymes: one that breaks down phosphatidylcholine to produce IP3 and diacylglycerol, and another that catalyses the opposite process, using a different substrate, to produce ATP and phosphatidylinositol.D = CORRECT - Phospholipase A2 is the specific enzyme which breaks down phosphatidylcholine to produce IP3 and arachidonic acid.E = incorrect - Phospholipase A1 is an enzyme that hydrolyses stored triglycerides into free fatty acids and glycerol. It is also sometimes calledlipoprotein lipase, as it is able to hydrolyse large triacylglycerol molecules to smaller ones. This enzyme is found in adipose tissue and is released when glucagon stimulates the liver. It hydrolyses the triglyceride stores in adipose tissue, and can therefore increase the availability of free fatty acids for beta-oxidation.This enzyme is produced by the group of cells known as adipocytes. Deficiency of this enzyme results in an inability to control the level of free fatty acids and hence may contribute to obesity. Excess is found in patients with diabetes. This was covered in the plenary on Lipids (Digestion, Absorption, Storage and Metabolism) in Case 6. https://teachmephysiology.com/biochemistry/lipids/prostaglandins/
best_explanation: Phospholipase A2 - PLA2 is the correct answer.This enzyme is involved in the first step of the production of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid. The arachidonic acid is cleaved from the membrane phospholipids by PLA2. The liberated arachidonic acid then becomes available for the synthesis of prostaglandins by the enzyme cyclooxygenase. A - Phospholipase B2, also called PLB2, is the second stage of the two stage process of the production of prostaglandins. It is activated by thrombin and catalyses the conversion of arachidonic acid into prostaglandin H2. B - Phospholipase B1, also called PLB1, is an enzyme that converts membrane phospholipid into IP3 and diacylglycerol. It is activated by thrombin as well. C - Phospholipase C is a different enzyme altogether. It is involved in signal transduction pathways, specifically in the cleavage of phospholipids to produce Ip3 and DAG. D - The first step of the production of prostaglandins from arachidonic acid. E - Phospholipase A1 is an enzyme that is involved in the breakdown of membrane phospholipids. It is activated by thrombin and is part of the first stage of the production of prostaglandins. These are just some of the enzymes involved in the production of prostaglandins. There are many more enzymes involved in the process and it is quite a complicated pathway. This was just a quick summary of the first two enzymes involved. I hope this was helpful! input: Given question: Sally has recently been experiencing a burning pain behind her sternum which is worse after eating and when lying down. After some of her own internet research she has decided to purchase some over the counter Gaviscon. She finds that this has helped relieve her symptoms, but the problem doesn't go away.  She goes to the GP, who diagnoses her with GORD and prescribes her omeprazole.  The GP tells her to stop taking the Gaviscon. Why is this? Option A: The internet is not an accurate source of medical advice. Gaviscon actually worsens the effects of GORD. Option B: Gaviscon is an enzyme inducer, therefore accelerating the metabolism of omeprazole. Option C: Omeprazole is a more effective drug, so there is no point taking Gaviscon as well. Option D: Omeprazole requires the acid environment of the stomach to be activated. The correct answer is Option D.
reference: https://geekymedics.com/why-you-shouldnt-combine-omeprazole-and-gaviscon/ For more information on this topic please refer to Dr Coffey's lecture from Case 1 Pharmacology of the Upper GI Tract. This was covered in the powerpoint under 'other drugs used to heal the oesophagus'. Also mentioned in the case 2 lecture on day 5. I hope this helps, let me know if you have any other questions. Love Sam :) (I am not a doctor, this is just my understanding from the lecture)
best_explanation: A- made up B- partially correct C- incorrect D- correct answer The enzyme inducer effect of Gaviscon would indeed accelerate the metabolism of omeprazole, however this would also reduce the effectiveness of the drug. This is because the drug would be broken down more quickly, so less of the full strength drug would reach the tissues where it is needed.  Gaviscon and omeprazole have different mechanisms of action, and can be used together to treat GORD. Gaviscon is an antacid which neutralises gastric acid in the oesophagus, whereas omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, reducing the amount of acid produced by the stomach in the first place.  However, if a patient is taking omeprazole they should not take Gaviscon as well because the antacid will interfere with the omeprazole.  The omeprazole needs to be activated by the acidic environment of the stomach to be converted into the active form of the drug.  If taken with an antacid, the activated form of omeprazole will be reduced, as the antacid reduces the acidity of the stomach, so the omeprazole will be less effective at reducing the amount of acid in the stomach. NSAIDs inhibit the secretion of prostaglandins, which normally protect the stomach from the effects of acid.  Prolonged use of NSAIDs greatly increases the risk of developing gastric ulcers.  Smoking, alcohol and obesity are known to increase the risk of developing gastric ulcers.  Stress is thought to be a cause of gastric ulcers, however this is not as proven as the other causes listed above.  This question is from the Upper GI Tract lecture from Case 1. input: Given question: During what stage of bone healing is RANK-L active? Option A: Bony callus formation Option B: Consolidation Option C: Granulation callus formation Option D: Inflammation Option E: Remodelling The correct answer is Option A.
reference: Rank L is a protein that is involved in osteoclasts, so it's active during bony callus formation when osteoclasts are resorbing the bone.  This information can be found in the 'Evolution of Structural Complexity' lecture from PCS unit 1.  For more details on bone healing and the different stages, I found this website very helpful: https://orthoinfo.org/conditions-and-treatments/bone-healing-process#:~:text=The%20first%20stage%2C%20inflammation%2C,formation%20begins%20(approximately%203).&text=The%20second%20stage%2C%20consoldiation%2C,can,dependently%20be%20seen%20on%20Xray.&text=The%20third%20stage%2C%20remodeling%2C,can,take,years%20to%20complete.&text=The%20final%20stage%2C%20radiussation,%20is,achieved%20when%20the%20bone%20has%20returned%20to%20its%20normal%20shape%20and%20strength.%20This%20may%20take%20several%20years.   I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any other questions.  :)%0A%0ABefore%20I%20went%20on%20holiday%20I%20searched%20up%20some%20of%20the%20lectures%20from%20PCS%20unit%201%20that%20I%20thought%20you%20might%20find%20useful%20so%20I%20can%27t%20remember%20all%20of%20it%20but%20I%20did%20find%20this%20out%20about%20RANK-L%20and%20bone%20healing.%20Hopefully%20you%20will%20find%20it%20helpful%20too:%0A%0Ahttps://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25496428%0AThis%20paper%20discusses%20how%20rankl%20gene%20deficiency%20impacts%20osteoclasts%20and%20bone%20healing.%20It%20mentions%20that%20RANK-L%20is%20involved%20in%20the%20activation%20of%20osteoclasts%20a%20during%20bone%20healing.%20It%20also%20discusses%20how%20rankl%20gene%20deficiency%20causes%20low%20turnover%20osteoprorsis%20and%20that%20this%20is%20related%20to%20reduced%20local%20bone%20turnover%20rather%20than%20systemic%20effects.%0A%0AThis%20information%20can%20be%20found%20in%20the%20'Evolution%20of%20Structural%20Complexity'%20lecture%20from%20PCS%20unit%201.%20For%20more%20details%20on%20bone%20healing%20and%20the%20different%20stages,%20I%20found%20this%20website%20very%20helpful:%20https://orthoinfo.org/conditions
best_explanation: The RANK-L is responsible for osteoclast differentiation and activation. Osteoclasts are large and multinucleated cells that are responsible for the resorption of bone. They are derived from monocytes and macrophages. During bone healing, osteoclasts are activated to resorb the bony callus, and RANK-L is responsible for this. It is also responsible for the differentiation of osteoclasts from monocytes and macrophages. In bony callus formation, osteoblasts migrate to the fracture site and start to produce an organic matrix (proteins and polysaccharides) around which they deposit calcium phosphate to form hydroxyapatite. RANK-L is also responsible for bony callus formation.  In consolidation, the hard callus is replaced by lamellar bone. In granulation callus formation, the soft callus is replaced by granulation tissue, which is made up of capillaries, fibroblasts, and macrophages. Inflammation is the initial response to injury and is characterized by increased vascularity, neutrophils, and mononuclear cells. In remodelling, the callus is replaced by newly formed bone, which is osteoblasts again.  Osteoblasts and osteoclasts have a reciprocal relationship. Osteoclasts resorb bone, and osteoblasts replace it. Osteoclasts are activated by RANK-L, and osteoblasts produce osteoprotegerin, which inhibits RANK-L. input: Given question: Poor James, a 5 year old boy, is brought to the GP by his mum who is concerned that he always seems more out of breath than the other children during sport and is often wheezy. You decide that the most likely diagnosis is asthma and prescribe Salbutamol. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of salbutamol? Option A: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor agonist Binds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinase Bronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option B: M3 receptor antagonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from binding This decreases cGMP production cGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option C: M3 receptor agonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from bindingThis decreases cGMP productioncGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option D: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor antagonistBinds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinaseBronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option E: Inhaled corticosteroid Binds to a glucocorticoid receptor Up regulates transcription anti-inflammatory mediatorsDown regulates transcription of inflammatory mediators Reduces inflammation The correct answer is Option A.
reference: The correct answer is A  Salbutamol is a sympathomimetic drug aka it mimics the sympathetic system effects. It acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the bronchioles and causes smooth muscle relaxation which widens the airways and reduces inflammation. This is opposite to salmeterol (inhaled anti-asthma drug) which acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the trachea and causes bronchodilation (widening of the airways) by causing mucus secretion and reducing inflammation. I found this website really helpful for explaining the mechanism of action of different types of asthma drugs http://www.asthma.org.uk/advice/treatment/drugs/long-acting-relievers/salmeterol-fluticasone/why-they-work#:~:text=The%20drug%20is%20absorbed%20into,causes%20bronchodilation%20by%20causing%20mucus%20secretion.&text=Salmeterol%20and%20fluticasone%20both,reduce%20inflammation%20in%20the%20airways.  I also found this video helpful as it explains the mechanism of action of salbutamol and how it differs from salmeterol https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tTgF9IH1fP8&t=466s (the explanation starts at 5:27)  Please note that I am not medically trained and this is all based on my own research, so please do not rely solely on this for your assessments.
best_explanation:
The correct answer is A!Salbutamol is a sympathomimetic drug aka it mimics the sympathetic system effects. It acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the bronchioles and causes smooth muscle relaxation which widens the airways and decreases inflammation. This is opposite to salmeterol which acts on the beta-2-adrenoreceptor in the central and peripheral nervous system and causes bronchodilation (dilates the airways) and decreases inflammation. I always remember beta-2-adrenoreceptor agonists as the 'blue' drugs as opposed to the 'white' druh- bronchodilators (like salmeterol) which are B2 antagonists (like ipratropium) or antihistamines.  B2 antagonists are usually given to patients with asthma as an alternative to salbutamol as they can be prescribed by a doctor and taken orally. reference: Testicular torsion is a twisting of the spermatic cord that causes the testicular artery to become occluded. This cuts off blood flow to the testis, causing ischemia (decrease in blood supply) which leads to necrosis of the testicular tissue. Since the testicular artery is occluded, the temperature in the scrotum rises rapidly because the arterial blood from the aorta is diverted into the epididymis and other structures in the scrotum instead of being distributed evenly throughout the scrotum. This rise in temperature causes edema (swelling) of the epididymis and the other structures in the scrotum, resulting in a swollen scrotum. Due to the loss of the testicular tissue, cessation of the HPG axis, and loss of the seminiferous tubules, the testes are never able to function normally again. Most commonly occurs in boys between the age of 10 and 16. Descending testes cannot be definitely prevented but the risk can be minimized by wearing athletic supporters rather than underpants. Boys who have had testicular torsion once are at a very high risk of having it happen again. Most males who have had testicular torsion will not have any children as a result of it, although some may have fertility problems. Most males who have had testicular torsion will require oral or IV corticosteroids (prednisolone) to try to save the testicle. Surgery is usually required if there is evidence of damage to the spermatic cord or the testicular artery has been occluded for more than 8 hours. Up to 12% of males with testicular torsion will develop infertility as a result of poor sperm production. Most males who experience testicular torsion will regain normal testicular function, but the likelihood of this decreases with increasing duration of ischemia. input: Given question: Joints have a rich nerve supply provided by articular nerves. Hilton's law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. The nerve of a joint transmits impulses which play a key role in which sense? Option A: Nociception Option B: Proprioception Option C: Exteroception Option D: Interoception Option E: Kinesthesia The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Hilton’s Law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. This means that the nerve of a joint transmits impulses which are related to proprioception. Proprioception is the sense of where your body is in space and time. It allows you to close your eyes and still move your limbs without bumping into things. It is mediated by articular nerves.  Nociception is the sensation of pain. It is mediated by A-delta fibres which are slow (10-20m/s) conducting fibres. They transmit signals of intense pain, often from damaged tissues.  Exteroception is the sensory system concerned with our awareness of stimuli in the environment, such as light touch, vibration, pressure etc. It is mediated by free nerve endings, which are found in the skin.  Interoception refers to the conscious perception of physiological responses or bodily feelings, such as hunger, thirst, fatigue or discomfort. It is not well understood, but it may involve afferent neurons that do not synapse in the spinal cord, but rather in the brain stem or higher brain regions.  Kinesthesia refers to the awareness of the movement of your own body. It is proprioception over longer periods, and so includes the ability to learn and remember motor skills.  For more information on this topic see the PCS unit 3 tutorial on ‘General sensation: what comes in via the special senses?’  Case 6: ‘The cutaneous sensations of the upper limb’, in ‘Clinical Skills for Lower Limb and Trunk Injuries’, will allow you to develop your skills in examining patients with SBS. input: Given question: Hypertension can be defined as persistent blood pressure greater than or equal to 140/90mmHg. There are many antihypertensive drugs including one called Losartan. What type of antihypertensive drug is Losartan? Option A: ACE inhibitor Option B: Angiotensin II receptor blocker Option C: Calcium channel blocker Option D: Beta blocker Option E: Thiazide like diuretic The correct answer is Option B.
reference: Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker so it works by preventing the action of angiotensin II. This prevents the kidneys from absorbing salt and water which reduces blood volume and therefore blood pressure.  A - ACE inhibitor such as Captopril work by preventing the formation of angiotensin II which reduces blood pressure.  C- Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil work by lowering the amount of calcium ions entering cardiac cells and blood vessel walls. This prevents the heart from contracting as strongly, and therefore reduces blood pressure.  D- Beta blockers such as Propranolol work by preventing the action of adrenaline. Adrenaline increases the strength of contraction of the heart, and therefore raised blood pressure.  E- Thiazide like diuretics such as Chlorothiazide remove excess salt from the body via the kidneys, this reduces blood viscosity and therefore blood pressure.  For more information on these drugs and their mechanisms refer to the pharmacology light bulb on LC. We also covered this in the case 6 pharmacology plenary.  Thanks for playing along! :)
best_explanation: B is the correct answer! Losartan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker so it works by preventing angiotensin II from binding to its receptor. This prevents the effects of angiotensin II which include vasoconstriction. This prevents the increase in blood pressure.  A- ACE inhibitor such as Captopril work by preventing the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. This reduces the amount of angiotensin II which means there is less vasoconstriction and hypertension is reduced. C- Calcium channel blockers such as Verapamil work by lowering the influx of calcium ions into cardiac cells and blood vessel walls. This prevents the hearts contractile force which means the heart has to work harder to pump the same amount of blood. This increase in workload on the heart means the heart does not have to contract as strongly and so the pressure is reduced.  D- Beta blockers such as Propranolol work by preventing the binding of norepinephrine to its receptor. This prevents the effects of norepinephrine which include increase in heart rate and contractile force of the heart. This means the heart has to work harder to pump the same amount of blood. This increase in workload on the heart means the heart does not have to contract as strongly and so the pressure is reduced.  E- Thiazide like diuretics such as Chlorothiazide remove excess water and salt from the body by making the kidneys excrete more H2O and Na+ ions. This reduces the volume of blood and so the pressure is reduced. This is a side effect and not the main mechanism of action. input: Given question: What would happen if a child had growth hormone in excess? Option A: Acromegaly Option B: Gigantism Option C: Dwarfism Option D: No effect The correct answer is Option B.
reference: If a child has growth hormone in excess they will develop gigantism. This means that the bones will grow faster than usual resulting in tall stature. However due to the fact that the epiphyseal plates are still open, the bones will continue to grow in length. In adults this condition is called acromegaly. It is caused by a pituitary tumour and results in tall stature and various other symptoms such as excessive sweating and diabetes.  Growth hormone deficiency in children will result in dwarfism. This is because there is an insufficient amount of growth hormone to stimulate the production of IGF-1 which in turn prevents the development of the bones and results in short stature. In adults it is called hypopituitarianism. It may be caused by damage to the pituitary gland, hypothyroidism or a tumour that affects the pituitary gland. There will be no effect on the body if there is an even amount of growth hormone. This is because growth hormone works on a pinpoint basis. It only affects the cells in its immediate area. Therefore if there is an even amount of growth hormone in the body there will be no noticeable effect. This was taken from the PCS 3 lecture on growth hormone. best_explanation: If a child has GH in excess they will develop gigantism.  In children growth hormone is secreted by the anterior pituitary.  The excess GH causes bones to grow faster so the child will get taller.  However, the bones will also stop growing at a normal rate.  This means that if the GH excess is not treated, the child will end up with a very tall adult height but with other problems such as a large head and hands, a depressed nasal bridge and an enlarged tongue.  If the GH excess is treated before bone growth is finished then the child can be helped to reach a normal adult height.  Gigantism is very rare and only happens in children.  Acromegaly happens when adults have GH excess.  The excess GH causes the same effects as in gigantism but the effects are less severe.  Adults with acromegaly are usually of normal height but they may be over 6ft tall.  They may have a protruding jaw, an enlarged tongue, a large nose and thick lips.  Their feet may be flat and their hands may be wide and short.  They may also develop diabetes mellitus, hypertension and cardiomyopathy.  The excess GH causes these problems because it causes the body to insulase more, which increases the amount of glucose in the blood.  The excess glucose causes diabetes mellitus and the extra glucose and insulin cause the other problems.  The excess GH also causes the arteries to thicken which increases the blood pressure.  The thickened heart muscle in the left ventricle can cause cardiomyopathy.  In summary, gigantism is very rare and only happens in children.  Acromegaly only happens in adults.  If a child has gigantism then they will grow very tall but the bones will stop growing at a normal rate.  This means that if the GH excess is not treated, the child will end up with a very tall adult height but with other problems such as a large head and hands, a depressed nasal bridge and an enlarged tongue.  If the GH excess is treated before bone growth is finished then the child can be helped to reach a normal adult height.

input: Given question: Our immunity can be divided into that which is Innate and that which is Adaptive, each comprising of different cell types, with different functions. reference: Dendritic cells are the link between innate and adaptive immunity as they have innate immunity characteristics (they present MHC/peptide complexes to naïve T cells) but also play a role in adaptive immunity by activating T and B lymphocytes. They are found near the skin and in tissues such as the lung, GI tract and urogenital tracts. They are derived from macrophages.  Adapted from Small Group Tutorial - Immunology (led by Prof Dave Wilson) and PCS Unit 2 Immune Response Lecture. best_explanation: Dendritic cells are the only cell type which can bridge the gap between innate and adaptive immunity. They have a large number of receptors on their surface to detect the presence of a pathogen, they then process antigens and present them on their surface in conjunction with a co-stimulatory molecule, allowing naïve T cells to recognize and respond to the pathogen. This T cell response is specific and adaptive. Mast cells, macrophages, neutrophils and natural killer cells are all associated with innate immunity, Mast cells release histamine, important in parasitic infections. Macrophages have a crucial role in the early stages of infection, they phagocytose pathogens and stimulate the production of inflammatory molecules. Neutrophils are recruited to the site of infection and their neutrophil elastase enzyme breaks down the pathogens' membranes. Natural killer cells are important in viral infections and can recognize and kill infected cells.  Information source: Applied immunology and microbiology post tutorial document. input: Given question: Paul has a cracking headache, so decides to take some aspirin. Aspirin is a non-competitive inhibitor of PGHS1 and 2 enzymes. In terms of kinetics, how is Vmax, Km and Kcat affected? Option A: Vmax will increaseKm will decreaseKcat will increase Option B: Vmax will decreaseKm will not changeKcat will decrease Option C: Vmax will not change Km will decreaseKcat will increase Option D: Vmax will increaseKm will not changeKcat will decrease Option E: Vmax will increaseKm will decreaseKcat will not change The correct answer is Option B.
reference: From the fact that aspirin is a non-competitive inhibitor, we know that it doesn't matter whether or not the enzyme is saturated with substrate - the inhibition will be the same. Therefore, Vmax will decrease because no matter how much substrate there is, the enzyme activity will be reduced by the presence of aspirin (so the maximum rate of reaction will be lower). Also, Km would decrease because the concentration of substrate that produces half of Vmax (i.e. Km) will be higher due to the presence of aspirin (which lowers Vmax). Finally, since aspirin is not a competitive inhibitor, Kcat will stay the same because the affinity of the enzyme for the substrate is unchanged. I made up all of the other answers - I hope this explanation helps! Let me know if you have any questions. Cheers, Sian.
best_explanation: B is correct - competitive inhibitors increase Km (there is a greater concentration of substrate), Vmax remains the same because no matter how much substrate there is, you can only have one enzyme-substrate complex, and Kcat doesn't change because the enzyme is still catalysing the reaction at the same rate.  A - incorrect - Vmax is the maximum rate of reaction with all active sites saturated. This will not increase as the more substrate there is, the more enzyme-substrate complexes that are formed.  C - incorrect - similar to A.  D - incorrect - Kcat is the catalytic constant and is a measure of the enzyme's affinity for the substrate (the lower the Kcat, the higher the affinity).  E - incorrect - similar to C.  Overall, the fact that aspirin is a non-competitive inhibitor (it binds to the enzyme itself) means that Vmax and Kcat won't be affected, but the substrate concentration (Km) will decrease because there will be a greater incentive to produce more enzyme (as more substrate is available).  Note that competitive inhibitors bind to the substrate, so Vmax and Km will increase (there is a greater concentration of substrate) but Kcat won't change because the enzyme is still catalysing the reaction at the same rate. reference:
The inferior part of the heart is the most likely place for an occlusion to occur. As the inferior vena cava is positioned here and it is also the lowest point in the heart, any emboli that find their way into the venous system are most likely to be deposited here. reference: 2:1 or 3:1 second degree heart block is when not all impulses reach the ventricles, so atrial depolarisation is not synchronised with ventricular depolarisation. there are three types of 2:1 block- Mobitz type 1, Mobitz type 2 and 2:1:1 (also called 2:2:1) Mobitz type 2 is when there is a delay in the conduction of the AV node and sometimes not all P waves are followed by a QRS complex. this means that occasionally (at a rate of about 25%) a QRS complex will be dropped. If the PR interval is prolonged this suggests that less than 10% of the impulses are getting through to depolarise the ventricles. As the RR interval increases, it suggests that more impulses are being conducted from the atria to the ventricles (ie- higher ejection fraction). What is the diagnosis?Answer:Radial nerve palsy causes wrist drop and loss in sensation over the dorsal surface of the hand. The thumb is also flexed at MCP due to paralysis of the thenar eminence. The thenar eminence is innervated by the median nerve. Since the median nerve innervates the thenar eminence, the muscles that are innervated by the median nerve (intrinsic muscles of the hand) will be affected. These muscles include the opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, and the abductor pollicis brevis. This includes the muscles responsible for extension at MCP and extension at IP. Case 3: Hyperacusis - Sensitivity to loud noise, can be caused by ear infections, head trauma, exposure to loud music/noise. Can result in pain and temporary hearing loss. Down’s syndrome)  Secondary to glaucoma, diabetes, alcohol or uveitis o Glaucoma – intraocular pressure needs to be checked. Primary open angle glaucoma is slow and painless. Risk of glaucomatous visual field loss is estimated to be around 15% for people aged 40–60 years, increasing to over 50% for those aged 65–80 years. World Health Organization estimates that by 2020, glaucoma will be the leading cause of blindness globally. Secondary glaucoma can be caused by;  Eye injury  Eye infections  Blood vessel damage (eg. retinal vein occlusion)  Uveitis  Di
best_explanation: The upper eyelid is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system. The superior tarsal muscle is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and a lesion in the superior cervical ganglion, which is part of the sympathetic trunk, will cause a loss of sympathetic innervation to the superior tarsal muscle. This will cause a partial drooping of the upper eyelid.  A: Incomplete or complete lesion of the occulomotor nerve (III)  B: Incomplete or complete lesion of the facial nerve (VII)  C: Incomplete or complete lesion of the trigeminal nerve (V)  NOTE: In Horner's syndrome, it is almost always a lesion of the superior cervical ganglion that causes the loss of sympathetic innervation to the upper eyelid. It could be a lesion of the trigeminal nerve (V) but that would cause a drooping of the lower eyelid and that is not part of Horner's syndrome. (Information from dr watson's lecture)

input: Given question: What is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation? Option A: periaqueductal gray Option B: thalamus Option C: dorsal horn of spinal cord Option D: nucleus raphe magnus Option E: reticular formation The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
Periaqueductal gray (PAG) is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation.The PAG sends descending projections to the dorsal horn and is the final pathway for the modulation of nociceptive sensory information. The PAG can inhibit or facilitate the release of substance P via interneurons that project to the dorsal horn. In this way it can influence the experience of pain.The dorsal horn of the spinal cord is where ascending sensory information from the body's tissues is processed and then sent to the brain for interpretation.The thalamus is the second relay station in the ascending pathways, receiving information from the dorsal horn and transmitting it to the somatosensory homunculus in the cerebral cortex.This information is then interpreted by the brain to determine the quality of the sensation, such as sharp/dull, aching etc.The nucleus raphe magnus is a part of the brainstem involved in the regulation of serotonin.Serotonin is important in the descending pain modulation system as it is a neurotransmitter used by the descending neurones projecting to the dorsal horn.  The reticular formation is a part of the brainstem involved in arousal and consciousness. It is not directly involved in pain modulation. information source; pain management lecture, PCS2 tutorial document, pain and nociception lecture, PCS1 tutorial document. references; McBeth, J. input: Given question: Emily Davies, a 19-year-old female, comes to A+E after sustaining an injury to her hand and is unable to oppose her thumb but can abduct it, which muscle is likely to be damaged? Option A: Flexor pollicis brevis Option B: Flexor digiti minimi brevis Option C: Adductor pollicis Option D: Opponens pollicis Option E: Abductor pollicis brevis The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Opposable thumb muscles -Emily can abduct (move away from midline) but not oppose (make close to midline) her thumb so opponens pollicis is damaged. -Flexor pollicis brevis and flexor digiti minimi brevis are both in the superficial layer of the anterior compartment of the hand and are responsible for flexion of the MCP joints. -Adductor pollicis is in the deep layer of the anterior compartment and is responsible for adduction (bring towards midline) of the thumb. -Abductor pollicis brevis is also in the superficial layer and is responsible for abduction (move away from midline) of the thumb. TIP-opposition vs abduction opposition=the ability to make close to midline in order to use the thumb as a thumb.abduction=the ability to move away from midline. eg if you put your thumb by your side and move it away from your side it's abduction. if you put your thumb by your side and move it closer to your thumb it's opposition.  reference https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/anterior-compartment/hand/opponens-pollicis/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/ Deltoid-A muscle located on the posterior side of the upper arm. It is one of the chief muscles of the rotator cuff. The deltoid is a large muscle with two heads (a superior and an inferior head) which are united by a common tendinous belly. The fibers of the deltoid are inserted into the tuberosity of the humerus.The main part of the deltoid muscle is located on the lateral border of the scapula above the teres minor. The deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve and its main function is to provide stability to the glenohumeral joint and assist in abduction of the arm. Damage to this muscle may occur from a fractured humerus or dislocation of the shoulder. Nerve damage to the axillary nerve may cause weakness and paralysis of the deltoid.https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/posterior-compartment/deltoid/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/  LATERAL COLLATORAL LIGAMENT-a band of connective tissue that surrounds and supports the lateral condyle of the humerus. It is attached to the humeral shaft at one end and the greater tubercle of the humerus at the other. Its main part lies beneath the teres minor muscle, and its anterior and posterior margins lie respectively 3 and 3.5 cm lateral to the articular margin of the humeral shaft. The ligament prevents posterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. This holds the humeral head tightly in the glenoid, thereby helping to stabilize the shoulder joint. A tear of this ligament is called a shoulder dislocation. A dislocation occurs when the force acting upon the glenohumeral joint is great enough to pull the humeral head from the glenoid. Dislocations generally occur in a forward direction; i.e., the humeral head is forced under the acromion process of the scapular. A dislocation can be reduced manually (by pressing the humeral head back into the glenoid), or surgery may be necessary. After a first-time dislocation, the glenohumeral joint is never truly "stable" again. The risk of future dislocations is always present.  Reference https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/joints/shoulder-joint/lateral-collateral-ligament/ and https://www.rchsd.org/health-articles/quadruple-shoulder-repair-surgery/  SUPRASPINATUS-a muscle of the rotator cuff, located superiorly and medially to the first rib. The supraspinatus is the most commonly torn muscle in the rotator cuff. It originates from the supraspinous fossa of the scapula above the teres minor and the great tubercle of the humerus. The tendons of the supraspinatus passes beneath the acromion process

input: Given question: ACE-I (ACE inhibitors) are used to treat hypertension. What does this block? Option A: Parathyroid hormone Option B: Bilirubin Option C: Aldosterone Option D: Angiotensin II Option E: Atrial natriuetic petide The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
ACE-I block the conversion of angiotensin I to II by plasma bradykinin. This prevents the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) from activating. RAAS increases salt and water retention which increases blood pressure. ACE-I are more effective when used with a low dose of a diuretic (water pill). Combining these two drugs removes excess fluid, which reduces blood pressure. ACE-I have few side effects but they can lower the white blood cell count and potentiate the effects of antibiotic. ACE-I are more suitable for people who are allergic to penicillan (penicillin), cephalosporins or sulphonamides. (Page 392, PCS unit 2) Importance of ACE-I: -They are more suitable for people who are allergic to penicillan (penicillin), cephalosporins or sulphonamides. -They remove excess fluid which reduces blood pressure. -They are more effective when used with a low dose of a diuretic (water pill). -They have few side effects. -They prevent the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) from activating. RAAS increases salt and water retention which increases blood pressure. (Page 392, PCS unit 2) Other drugs that treat hypertension: -Calcium channel blockers -beta blockers -Diuretics -Vasodilators -Central acting agents Importance of addressing hypertension: -It is the single most important risk factor for cardiovascular disease -it causes left ventricular hypertrophy -it makes the heart work harder to pump blood -it damages blood vessels and leads to stroke and myocardial infarction -it causes target organ damage leading to chronic kidney disease and heart failure (page 387-8, PCS unit 2)

best_explanation: ACE-I block the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, thus reducing the amount of angiotensin II, and therefore less angiotensin I to II conversion is done. This means less Angiotensin II to be dealt with by the RAS (renin angiotensin system) which in turn results in less sodium reabsorption and hydrostatic pressure is reduced. Hence, blood pressure is reduced. input: Given question: Mr Vallance is having his tooth extracted. It is decided he needs a local anaesthetic which inhibits fast-gated sodium channels. Which one of the following medications is suitable? Option A: Diazepam Option B: Propofol Option C: Amobarbital Option D: Lignocaine Option E: Nitrous oxide The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Lignocaine (or lidocaine) is a amino amide local anaesthetic that inhibits fast-gated sodium channels. It is also used as an antiarrhythmic and as a stabiliser of the neuronal membrane. It is volatile and can be used with nitrous oxide as a vapour. Nitrous oxide is a weak vasodilator and lignocaine is a mild beta adrenoreceptor agonist so their interaction causes a slight decrease in blood pressure. Nitrous oxide has a very short half life and works quickly so is useful for minor surgery. The other options are all central nervous system depressants; diazepam is a benzodiazepine, propofol is a dissociative anaesthetic and amobarbital (also known as Amytal) is a barbiturate. These work by enhancing GABAergic activity. They have a high therapeutic index i.e. it takes a lot to overdose but they have a high risk of addiction and withdrawal symptoms. Nitrous oxide is very safe and has no major side effects or risks when used correctly.  All these drugs can be used as premedication before surgery. However, as fast-gated Na+ channels are also located in cardiac myocytes, the use of these drugs will also stop the heart. So unless there is an emergency, the above drugs cannot be used for this purpose.  I took most of this information from Dr Coffey's pharmacology light bulb. He always says "if it's not funny it's because it's true" so I hope this was helpful! Let me know if you want any more detail on anything :) xxxx

Nitrous oxide is a fast-gated sodium channel blocker and so would not be suitable for this procedure. The other options are all central nervous system depressants and so would not be suitable for this procedure.  A and B are both benzodiazepines and so act on the GABAergic system.C is a barbiturate and so acts on the GABAergic system. E is a gas anaesthetic and so acts on the central nervous system. input: Given question: A patient comes into A&E with an injured left knee. She was running an ultra marathon when she changed direction and felt a 'pop' in her knee. An MRI confirms what the orthopaedic consultant suspects is the likely diagnosis from the patient history and medical record-the patient tells the consultant that she has done this injury for the third time now. What is the most likely diagnosis and best treatment for the patient? Option A: ACL tear and non-operative therapy program of 6 to 8 weeks Option B: ACL tear and operative therapy program of 6 to 9 months Option C: PCL tear and operative therapy program of 6 to 9 months Option D: PCL tear and non-operative program of 6 to 8 weeks Option E: A stable patella fracture and non-perative therapy program of 6 to 8 weeks The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
30 points for answering the question correctly, 10 bonus points if you can provide the mechanism of injury (how does this happen?) and 20 bonus points if you can explain why this is a frequently recurring injury for this patient (what is the root cause?). A= incorrect, this is not the most likely diagnosis, although this could be correct for some patients with an ACL tearB= correct, this is the most likely diagnosis given the patient history and mechanism of injury, and the patient will require surgery due to the size of the tibial tunnel needed for the ACL graftC= incorrect, this is not the most likely diagnosisD= incorrect, this is not the most likely diagnosisE= incorrect, this is not the most likely diagnosismechanism of injury: the patient is running an ultra marathon and changes direction suddenly. This puts huge amounts of stress on the knee joint, and can cause the ACL to rupture. The patient may also have damaged their PCL as well. Root cause: the patient has a mechanical instability of the knee, which causes the ACL to rupture. This can be due to poor technique when changing direction, or a predisposition to valgus (inward) collapse of the knee. This can be improved upon with proper rehabilitation, but may remain a problem throughout the patients life. This patient may also benefit from learning how to change direction properly to prevent this injury happening again.

best_explanation: Most likely diagnosis: ACL tearTreatment: Operative therapy program of 6 to 9 months The patient has an anterior cruciate ligament tear. This is one of the most common injuries of the knee. The ACL provides structural stability to the knee joint. The patient has a history of this injury. This makes the diagnosis more likely. ACL tears can often be treated with bracing and physical therapy. However, many athletes, especially those who are highly active, choose surgery. Surgery involves reconstructing the ACL using a tendon from the patient's own body (autograft) or a tendon from a donor (allograft). The graft is then fixed in place with screws or anchors. The knee is then rehabilitated for 6-9 months. If the patient is very active and the knee is unstable, the surgery is usually advised. Non-operative therapy program of 6 to 8 weeks:This would be for a patient with a PCL tear or a stable patella fracture. PCL tears are less common than ACL tears, but they do occur. The PCL provides structural stability to the knee joint. PCL tears can often be treated with bracing and physical therapy. However, many athletes, especially those who are highly active, choose surgery. Surgery involves reconstructing the PCL using a tendon from the patient's own body (autograft) or a tendon from a donor (allograft). The graft is then fixed in place with screws or anchors. input: Given question: Mast cells are cellular components of the innate immune response and are important to wound healing and defence against pathogens via an inflammatory response. Which of the following chemicals is released by mast cells to dilate vessel walls and make vessels more permeable? Option A: Cytokines Option B: IL-1 Option C: Interferons Option D: Prostaglandins Option E: TNFalpha The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Prostaglandins cause vasodilation and increase vascular permeability. They are derived from arachidonic acid and are involved in many physiological processes including reproduction, inflammation and pain.  Allergic reactions also involve the release of prostaglandins.  Cytokines - signaling molecules that have a low molecular weight and are used extensively in intracellular communication. Examples include IL-1 and TNF alpha Interferons - a group of signaling proteins which are released by cells in response to viral or bacterial infections. They are named according to their function, with interferon types I, II, and III all being involved in antiviral responses.  TNF alpha - a cytokine that regulates cell proliferation and differentiation, as well as inflammation and apoptosis. It can cause vasodilation but is more known for its ability to cause vasoconstriction.  Other Important mast cell chemicals include histamine (which causes vasodilation and contributes to an inflammatory response through increased capillary permeability) and tryptase (a metalloproteinase that can cleave proteases and contribute to inflammation).  Refer to Case 6 Anatomy workbook 2 on innate immunity for more detail on mast cells and their functions.  Also, a good way to remember this is prostaglandins start with a P and are derived from arachidonic acid, while everything else starts with an C (cytokine, histamine, tryptase) and are involved in inflammation/immunity.  Hope this helps! input: Given question: Neurotransmitters are vital chemicals for communication between neurones and span a variety of responsibilities. Which major class of these chemicals are considered responsible for things like consciousness, attention, cognition and emotion? Option A: Amino acid neurotransmitters Option B: Monoamines Option C: Catecholamines Option D: Peptide neurotransmitters The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Consciousness, attention, cognition and emotion are all functions of the monoamine neurotransmitters, which include serotonin, histamine, dopamine and norepinephrine. These neurotransmitters act on axons with gaps between their terminal buttons (synapse). This type of synapse is called a chemical synapse. A - Amino acid neurotransmitters are responsible for functions such as stimulating muscles (e.g. acetylcholine), transmitting information through sensory organs (e.g. glutamate) and modulating pain (e.g. endorphins). They act on cells that have receptors embedded in the membrane. B - Catecholamines refer to two monoamines; Dopamine and norepinephrine. Their names come from the fact that they have a benzene ring and a double bond (hence catechol) and that they are amines (NH2). They act on the sympathetic nervous system, being responsible for the fight or flight response. C- Peptide neurotransmitters are made up. D- All neurotransmitters are involved in some way with physiology and behaviour, but some are more 'major' than others. The categories above are not exhaustive, and there are many other classes of neurotransmitter, e.g. hormones (adrenaline, thyroid hormone), local anaesthetics (tetracaine) and neuropeptides (substance P, substance K). It is worth noting that some neurotransmitters can fit into multiple categories; serotonin, for example, is both an amino acid and a monoamine. See the PCS 3 lecture on Chemical Communication for more detail.

input: Given question: Which of the following is not a cause of amnesia? Option A: Ageing Option B: Alzheimer's disease Option C: Anoxia or hypoxia Option D: Herpes simplex encephalitis Option E: Korsakoff syndrome The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
Amnesia can be caused by: - Certain medications - Trauma - Substance abuse - Infections such as herpes - Hypoxia/anoxia - Korsakoff Syndrome - Depression/schizophrenia - Head trauma - Stress - Alzheimer's disease - Stroke  Ageing is not a cause of amnesia, although memory loss is more common in older people due to age related decline in cognitive function.  Link to case 4 auditory pathways lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkC1vZaUpxs&t=259s (from 13 mins)  Link to case 6 semantic dementia lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S8wWr92Kiqw (from 23 mins)  Link to case 7 stroke lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YHHDJ0TkPXQ (from 21 mins)
==============================================================================================================  This was taken from the case 7 lecture on stroke and is a useful summary of different types of amnesia: There are different types of amnesia depending on what causes it. There are 2 main types: Anterograde – meaning memory loss that affects new memories. This is more common An example would be caused by head trauma or a strokeRetrograde – meaning memory loss that mainly affects old memories. This is less common Examples include; Korsakoff’s syndrome, alcoholic memory loss, herpes simplex virus infection, hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia, alzheimers  Another type is temporary amnesia which can be caused by; trauma, stress, seizures, severe emotional distress, oxygen deprivation, ingestion of certain drugs, alcohol withdrawal, sleep disorders, hyperventilation, head injury, hypoglycemia, hyperthyroidism  All these different causes have one thing in common – they cause disruption to short term memory. Memory loss can be either retrograde (prior to illness/injury) or anterograde (after illness/injury). Sometimes there is a reversible cause e.g. vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency, hypercalcemia. Sometimes it is irreversible e.g. anoxia/hypoxia, traumatic brain injury, bleeding into the brain/around the brain.  People often confuse dementia with amnesia but they are not the same thing. Dementia is a broader term that describes a decline in cognitive function that is so severe it interferes with daily life. Memory loss is just one symptom of dementia. For example someone may have vascular dementia where they have had a series of mini-strokes which causes memory loss but they may still remember things from before their illness. Whereas with Korsakoff syndrome the patient will have difficulty recalling both recent and past memories.  Case 6 lecture on semantic dementia highlighted how memory loss can be profound yet the person is often aware of this and finds it very distressing. They may know what they want to say but the words aren’t there. It is thought that semantic dementia may be the most common form of early onset dementia. input: Given question: A 25 year old women came at the A&I with a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus. What is the most likely nerve she damaged because of the fracture? Option A: Ulnar nerve Option B: Musculocutanous nerve Option C: Median nerve Option D: Axillary nerve Option E: Long thoracic nerve The correct answer is Option D.
reference:
The axillary nerve passes medially to the surgical neck of the humerus and may be damaged by a fracture at this area. Symptoms of this would include weakness and loss of sensation in the shoulder region. A-Ulnar nerve does not pass close to the surgical neck of the humerusB-Musculocutanous nerve is posterior to the surgical neckC-Symptoms of a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus would not suggest muscle wasting or colour changes (musculocutanous nerve)D-The axillary nerve passes medially to the surgical neck of the humerus so it is most likely to be damagedE-Long thoracic nerve does not pass close to the surgical neck of the humerus either. This nerve damage will result in paralysis to the serratus anterior muscle which pulls the scapulae outwards. Therefore resulting in a winged scapula. There would also be weakness in the upper arm. Winged Scapula: https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/back/serratus-anterior/winged-scapula/ (Note the downward pull on the scapulae by the serratus anterior would normally keep the costal surface of the scapulae closely apposed to the ribs. When this muscle is paralysed, the scapulae are no longer held against the ribs, and are instead pulled away from the ribs by the deltoid and trapezius muscles.) https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/injuries/fractures/surgical-neck-fracture/ (The surgical neck is the most common site of fracture of the humerus; it is an area of weakness caused by a narrowing of the bone. Fractures here often occur when falling on an outstretched hand. The ends of the broken bones may push through the skin. It is important to get medical attention immediately if this happens. Surgery may be needed to repair the damage.)
It is important to always consider nerve damage when there is a fracture at the surgical neck of the humerus. The axillary nerve is most likely to be damaged. Damage to this nerve will result in weakness and loss of sensation in the shoulder region. In addition, it may cause paralysis to the deltoid and teres minor muscles. Since these muscles are responsible for abducting the arm past 15 degrees from the midline, this would result in a condition known as "claw hand" where the arm cannot be abducted past 15 degrees from the midline. Furthermore, it may cause a loss of sensation over the regimental badge area. http://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/nerves/axillary/ - This website has great information on the axillary nerve including its function, innervation and possible lesions. This means that the cardiac output is reduced, which can lead to shock and death if untreated. As well as this, the decreased space within the heart makes it harder for the heart to fill with blood. Pericardial effusion is the build up of fluid in the pericardial cavity. This can be caused by a range of factors, including inflammation of the pericardium, heart failure and cancer.  Tension pneumothorax is the build up of air in the pleural cavity causing an increase in pressure, which in turn causes an inward movement of the thoracic wall. This makes it harder for the heart to fill with blood, and can lead to cardiac arrest. Pericarditis is the inflammation of the pericardium. The cause of this can be unknown, or it can be caused by a range of factors such as infection, cancer, or radiation therapy. Pericarditis can lead to an increase in pressure within the heart, as described in cardiac tamponade. However, pericarditis can also lead to an abnormal heart rhythm, as the electrical impulses of the heart are altered due to the inflammation.  Hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions.

input: Given question: Upon fertilisation what hormone is produced by a developing embryo prior to placenta formation? Option A: Progesterone Option B: Oestrogen Option C: hCG Option D: GNRH The correct answer is Option C.
reference:
During the early stages of development before the placenta forms, it is the developing embryo that produces hCG. This is important as it prevents the mother's immune system from rejecting the developing embryo as foreign tissue. Once the placenta is developed enough to produce progesterone and oestrogen, the developing embryo stops producing hCG. However, hCG can still be detected in the mother's blood because it has crossed the placenta. Later on, when the placenta is fully developed, it is the placenta that produces hCG. hCG is also produced in males to stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone  Practical application:   hCG is used in assisted reproduction techniques such as IVF. It can be given to the mother to take orally or can be administered via injection. It is also used to boost low amh levels in women undergoing ivf due to low oestrogen levels. It can also be given to men to boost tesosterone levels if they have low sperm counts.   Reference: Case 6 Anatomy Practical - Reproductive Health
Another useful website is: https://www.fertile-health.info/hcg-injections.html   Extra Info:   When a fertilised egg implants into the uterine lining, it is the placenta that begins to produce hormones such as progesterone and oestrogen. These hormones maintain the endometrium and allow it to thicken to support the developing foetus. After the placenta is formed, the developing embryo (now called a foetus) no longer produces hCG but the placenta continues to do so.  Prior to the development of the placenta, the developing embryo produces hCG to prevent the mother's immune system from rejecting the developing foetus as foreign tissue. This is because the mother's immune system does not yet recognise the developing foetus as a 'self' cell. Instead, it recognises the embryo as a foreign object and would attempt to destroy it. The hCG tricks the mother's immune system into thinking that the developing foetus is indeed a part of her own body and therefore should not be attacked. This was covered in the reproductive anatomy lecture in case 4.  Later on, once the placenta is developed enough, it is the placenta that produces hCG. This is because the placenta has a much greater capacity for producing hormones than the developing embryo. Even though the developing embryo no longer produces hCG, hCG can still be detected in the mother's blood because it has crossed the placenta. This was covered in the reproductive hormones lecture in case 5.  Lastly, hCG is also produced in males to stimulate Leydig cells to produce testosterone. Leydig cells are found in the testicles and are responsible for producing testosterone. If a male has low levels of testosterone, hCG can be administered to stimulate the production of Leydig cells which will then produce testosterone. This was covered in the reproductive hormones lecture in case 5.
best_explanation: Before the formation of the placenta, the developing embryo produces hCG to maintain the corpus luteum and its production of progesterone. After the formation of the placenta, oestrogen and progesterone are produced by the placenta and the corpus luteum respectively.  hCG maintains the corpus luteum by preventing its programmed cell death. It is the placenta that produces oestrogen and progesterone.  Note that GNRH is the hormone released by the hypothalamus that stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete the gonadotropins FSH and LH.  FSH and LH are the hormones that stimulate the development of Leydig cells in the testes, which produce testosterone.  Progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum and the placenta. Progesterone maintains the endometrium and is essential for the implantation and development of the embryo.  Oestrogen is also produced by the placenta. Oestrogen maintains the endometrium and is essential for the development of the embryo. Oestrogen also plays an important role in female sexual function and arousal.  hCG is a hormone released by the placenta when levels of maternal IgG reach a certain concentration in the blood. hCG prevents the mother's immune system from rejecting the foetus as foreign. hCG also has a role in maintaining the corpus luteum and is thus essential for the maintenance of progesterone secretion during the early stages of pregnancy. input: Given question: Which pathway of the complement system is activated by antibodies? Option A: Alternative Option B: Classical Option C: Opsonisation Option D: Mannan Lectin Option E: Membrane Attack Complex The correct answer is Option B.
reference: The Classical Pathway is activated by antibody-antigen complexes on invading bacteria. The other pathways are activated by different mechanisms. See the Case 6 Immunology lecture and tutorial for more detail. This was also in the learning outcomes from the plenary on Complement System & Lectin Pathway in Case 5. Resources: - Applied immunology and microbiology post tutorial document (led by Prof Dave Wilson) - Case 6 immunology lecture - Learning outcome from plenary on Complement System & Lectin Pathway - Handout from lecture on Complement System: Functions & Clinical Importance (led by Dr John Wilson) Link to lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CMZ2AormwgU&t=4178s See section 3 for antibodies and alternative pathway. See section 4 for classical pathway. See section 5 for lectin pathway. See section 6 for mannan lectorin. See section 7 for membrane attack complex. Note that there are some overlapping functions. E.g. Mannan Lectin Pathway is also involved in opsonisation. The functions are not mutually exclusive. The lecturer emphasised that this is a very complicated area and it's difficult to be comprehensive. He recommended focusing on the basic science behind why something works rather than trying to memorise everything. I.e. focus on understanding the genetics and molecules involved rather than just rote learning. He also said that there would be many things that we don't know or aren't sure about yet. He encouraged us to do primary literature research to find out more. There are also good online resources such as immunology.org and the microanatomy website. He also recommended the book "immunology and microbiology" by shauna downs which is available on leeds learn. He said that the most important thing is to have a broad general knowledge of immunology and then to specialise in areas we are interested in.
best_explanation: Classical is activated by antibodies, the rest are activated by binding to microbial surfaces Alternative is a spontaneous C3 hydrolysis into the formation of C3b, a C3 convertase is formed which converts C3 into C3a and C3b, the C3b can then go on to form C5 convertase with the help of a co-factor.  Opsonisation occurs spontaneously in the plasma, C3b combines with a pathogen and forms a “bacteria-complement” complex, this increases phagocytosis.  Mannan Lectin is a protein in the plasma, when it binds to a microbial surface, it activates the classical pathway.  Membrane Attack Complex is a C5b-coated bacterium, C5a combines with other proteins to produce terminal components of the inflammatory response, C3 convertase is formed, leading to cell lysis.  (From Applied immunology and microbiology post tutorial document) PCS Unit 2 Little bit of background on immunity: There are three main branches of defence in the immune system: 1. Innate – a rapid response to infection, macrophages and neutrophils phagocytose (process of opsonisation) pathogens, complement system (classical and alternative) 2. Adaptive – T and B lymphocytes are specific to a pathogen, activated T kills infected cells, B produces antibodies for the complement system 3. Acquired – specific immunity, T and B lymphocytes are specific to a pathogen, activated T kills infected cells, B produces antibodies for the complement system (From PCS unit 1) Little bit of background on complement system: The complement system is a biochemical pathway within the blood that works with the immune system to help eliminate invading bacteria and viruses. The complement system is activated by microbial surfaces and works with phagocytes to help identify and kill microorganisms. There are three main pathways in the complement system: classical, lectin, and alternative. The classical pathway is activated by antibodies, the lectin pathway is activated by binding to a microbial surface

reference: The presence of antibodies to the HBV surface protein indicates previous exposure to the virus and immunity, whereas the absence of these antibodies indicates an acute/recent infection. In this case, since only the anti-HBs antibody is present, this would indicate that the patient is currently infected with HBV but NOT Hep D. Also, as the IgM is negative, this rules out acute Hep BBoth Hep B and Hep D can occur simultaneously, however, they are two distinct viral infections that require different mechanisms of action to be diagnosed. reference: 4 of the rotator cuff muscles insert at the greater tubercle. The 5th inserts at the lesser tubercle. Therefore the one that inserts at the lesser tubercle is subscapularis. input: Given question: A young male child is brought into the clinic. His mother says that he bleeds easily and has bleeding joints characterised by stiffness, pain swelling and heat. You suspect haemophilia A and decide to carry out a test for the intrinsic pathway. What test should you carry out ? Option A: PT Option B: APTT Option C: CT Option D: ATP The correct answer is Option B.
reference: APTT would be expected to be very prolonged in haemophilia A as Factor VIII is deficient/missing so the intrinsic pathway is activated and takes much longer to consume the substrate (collagen). This is one of the tests carried out for haemophilia along with a test for factor VIII levels. There is also a test for factor IX levels which would be abnormal in haemophilia B. Haemophilia A & B are X linked recessive disorders. symptoms for haemophilia C are less severe and it is caused by a deficiency/malfunction of factor XIV. Haemophilia A, B & C all result in uncontrolled bleeding. Haemophilia A & B are inherited through a mutation on the X chromosome where as haemophilia C is not inherited but is instead caused by a spontaneous mutation in the gene. refer to dr watson's lecture on haemostasis and blood clotting from case 2. also refer to jeff allen's upper gi case 6 planery cell dysfunction for more detailed information on haemophilia.  http://www.hematology.org.uk/blood-disorders/haemophilia.html  http://www.nhs.uk/conditions/Haemophilia/Pages/Introduction.aspx   http://www.patient.co.uk/doctor/haemophilia-types-and-symptoms     http://www.rchsd.org/health-articles/q-a-haemophilia/#:~:text=Haemophilia%20is%20a%20genetic%20disease%2C%20in,activated%20by%20trauma%20or%20infection.&text=A%20defect%20in%20factor%20XII%20means,carried%20out%20to%20determine%20if%20it%20is%20present.%20(APTT)%20test%20will%20be%20prolonged.%20This%20will%20take%20longer%20than%20the%20activated%20by%20trauma%20or%20infection.%20This%20is%20one%20of%20the%20tests%20carried%20out%20for%20haemophilia%20along%20with%20a%20test%20for%20factor%20VIII%20levels.%20There%20is%20also%20a%20test%20for%20factor%20IX%20levels%20which%20would%20be%20abnormal%20in%20haemophilia%20B.%20Haemophilia%20A%20&%20B%20are%20X%20linked%20recessive%20disorders.%20Symptoms%20for%20haemophilia%20C%20are%20less%20severe%20and%20it%20is%20caused%20by%20a%20deficiency%2Fmalfunction%20of%20factor%20XIV.%20Haemophilia%20A,%20B%20&%20C%20all%20result%20in%20uncontrolled%20bleeding.%20Haemophilia%20A%20&%20B%20are%20inherited%20through%20a%20mutation%20on%20the%20X%20chromosome%20whereas%20haemophilia%20C%20is%20not%20inherited%20but%20is%20instead%20caused%20by%20a%20spontaneous%20mutation%20in%20the%20gene.%20refer%20to%20dr%20
best_explanation: APTT will test the intrinsic pathway as it is a prolonged bleeding time test. PT is a test for the extrinsic pathway as it is a one stage test for fibrin formation.  CT is a test for fibrin degradation. ATP is a test for the presence of ATP which is found in the intrinsic pathway.  Haemophilia A is a disease of the intrinsic pathway as it is a fibrinogen deficiency. Haemophilia B is a disease of the extrinsic pathway as it is a factor IX deficiency. Haemophilia C is a disease of the intrinsic pathway as it is a factor XIV deficiency. reference:
Alpha 1 Adrenoceptors are found in the heart and act to decrease heart rate and blood pressure.Phenylephrine is an agonist of these receptors and so it has an effect similar to adrenaline. This drug is used to test for alpha 1 adrenoceptor blockade (e.g. to assess if a patient is taking an alpha 1 antagonist drug).  I formed this question based on the pharmacology lightbulb case 2 on the cardiac physiology workshop. For more information on this see the case 2 pharmacology document under the 'drug' tab. I will put up a separate question on the beta adrenoceptors at some point in the future. Let me know if you want me to remind you when I do this. Cheers, Alex.
best_explanation: Alpha 1 adrenoceptors are found in the heart and the alpha 2 adrenoceptors are found in the blood vessels.  Phenylephrine is an agonist of alpha 1 adrenoceptors and so it acts to increase the heart rate and contractility of the heart.  The other 4 drugs are agonists of alpha 2 adrenoceptors and so they act to dilate the blood vessels and lower the blood pressure. input: Given question: Mannose & Fucose are carbohydrates found on the cell wall of bacteria. What aspect of the complement system do they activate? Option A: C3b Option B: Classical pathway Option C: Lectin pathway Option D: C3a Option E: Alternative pathway The correct answer is Option C.
reference: https://teachmephysiology.com/immune-system/innate-immune-system/complement-system/ This website explains the 3 ways in which mannose and fucose activate lectin pathway. 1) by binding to a protein on the surface of invading bacteria 2) by binding to a protein on the surface of fungi 3) by binding to a protein on the surface of viruses (not all viruses have this so not all viral infections will be detected) It also explains that once activated, a cascade occurs where C3 convertase is activated which results in downstream effects. One of these is the production of C3a and C5a which are anaphylatoxins - these stimulate mast cells and basophils to release histamine and other proinflammatory substances. Another effect is the formation of C5b which can bind to the surface of invading organisms and trigger macrophages and neutrophils to phagocytose (process of opsonisation) them.  This website is quite detailed so if you're interested in learning more, I recommend having a look! :)  Tutorial: Innate Immunity & Complement System (led by Prof Dave Wilson) & Complement System (led by Prof Graham Lord) both in Case 4. There is also a short powerpoint in the immunology folder in case 4 on the basics of the complement system. I also found the PCS unit 2 lecture on innate immunity and the complement system really helpful. Let me know if you want the link to any of those resources! :)
best_explanation: Mannose & Fucose are lectin pathway activators (They are found on the pathogen cell wall, so when they are recognised by the complement system, it activates the lectin pathway) C3a & C3b are products from the three complement pathways (Lectin, Classical & Alternative) C3a is an anaphylatoxin, which stimulates immune response (e.g. histamine release from mast cells) C3b is a opsonin, which helps phagocytosis  (It also helps trigger the C3 convertase, which then activates other complement pathways)  FYI: The Lectin Pathway is spontaneous C3 hydrolysis into the formation of C3b, which then acts as a opsonin.  The Classical Pathway is activated when a MHC class 3 molecule binds to a microbial antigen, then a C3 convertase is activated. input: Given question: What epithelial cell type functions as a mediator of filtration and diffusion? Option A: simple squamous Option B: simple cuboidal Option C: simple columnar Option D: stratified squamous Option E: pseudostratified The correct answer is Option A.
reference: simple squamous - as the name suggests, these cells are simply shaped with a single layer of cells which function as a physical barrier to prevent the passage of negatively charged ions. Simple cuboidal - function as a site of active absorption simple columnar - specialised for secretion/production of mucus/cells simple cuboidal/stratified cuboidal - sites of active absorption and secretion pseudostratified - found in the respiratory tree; each cell is connected to the basal lamina by a gap junction and the epithelium appears 'pseudostratified' because the cells are arranged at roughly equal distances from each other, giving the appearance of layers. However, each cell is actually connected to several other cells in the layer immediately beneath it. This arrangement allows for expansion/contraction without the layers themselves moving. (from microanatomy workbook answers) filtration and diffusion lecture PCS Unit 1 Little bit of extra information that might be helpful: the apical surface of simple squamous epithelial cells face the lumen of the tubule/duct whereas the basal surface is attached to the basement membrane. The lateral surfaces are free to move and can contract/expand To allow for diffusion to occur, specific transporters must be present on the plasma membrane. For example, Na+/K+ ATPase pump will remove Na+ after it has been filtered into the tubule/duct and K+ will diffuse back into the cell down its concentration gradient. Na+ will then diffuse back into the cell when it's concentration is higher on the outside. (Diffusion lecture PCS unit 1) also the following video is very helpful and easy to understand: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CMZ2AormwgU (10 mins)

input: Given question: Jim's just gotten a new iPhone and is playing around with portrait mode on the camera app. The way the camera is able to focus on a nearby object and blur out objects in the distance reminds him of how the human eye works in a similar way. The ciliary muscle in the eye controls accommodation for viewing objects at varying distances. Which cranial nerve innervates this muscle? Option A: Ophthalmic nerve (branch of CN V trigeminal nerve) Option B: Optic nerve (CN II) Option C: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) Option D: Abducens nerve (CN VI) Option E: Trochlear nerve (CN IV) The correct answer is Option C.
reference: C is correct! The oculomotor nerve supplies motor function to the superior, inferior and medial rectus (the 3 main 'muscles' of the eyeball), as well as parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle (which controls accommodation), and the levator palebrae (which acts to close the eyelids).  A - although the ophthalmic nerve (a branch of the trigeminal CN V) does have sensory innervation to the cornea, it doesn't actually supply any motor function to the eye itself. B - Although the optic nerve does receive visual information from the retina, it doesn't actually control any muscles within the eye itself.D & E - These two nerves don't even innervate any parts of the eye at all! D is quite tricky as the abducens nerve does give motor innervation to the lateral rectus muscle of the eyeball, but C is still more correct as it also gives parasympathetic innervation to the ciliary muscle. E - The trochlear nerve only has motor innervation to one muscle - the superior oblique muscle of the eyeball, but while this is technically correct, it's not as accurate as C which covers both the ciliary muscle AND the levator palpebrae.

A - this would decrease the amount of glucose entering cells and so the amount of glucose in the blood would be increased. B - this would take longer for glucose to enter the cells and so the amount of glucose in the blood would be increased. C - this is what growth hormone does to increase the level of glucose in the blood. D - this is a result of the action of growth hormone. E - this is another result of the action of growth hormone.
