Jerry's case of acromegaly is quite rare but diabetes caused by growth hormone excess is more common in menopausal women and is one of the causes of non-insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). Diabetics can suffer from hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar) and hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar). Hyperglycaemia occurs when your body cannot make enough insulin or when your cells do not respond to insulin. This means glucose stays in your blood and doesn't get into your cells. Over time, high blood sugar can lead to serious problems with your eyes, feet, kidneys, nerves, and teeth. Hypoglycaemia happens when your body makes too much insulin or when your cells become too sensitive to insulin. This causes your blood sugar to drop lower than normal. Hypoglycaemia is more likely to occur in people with diabetes who use insulin to control their blood sugar.

best_explanation:
GH increases gluconeogenesis and lypolysis in adipose tissue.  When stimulated by growth hormone, the liver produces glucose by the enzyme gluconeogenesis, from non-carbohydrate sources such as pyruvate and glycerol.  GH also causes an increase in lipolysis in adipose tissue, so fat is broken down to release free fatty acids which can then be used to make new glucose.  This all results in an increase of glucose in the blood.  The slower rate of glycolysis and decreased number of GLUT1 transporters that occur as a result of GH are both secondary effects, and the result of the increased levels of glucose in the blood.  In people who are insulin resistant, as a result of diabetes, the decreased rate of glycolysis means that less glucose is available to the cells, making them more resistant to insulin.  The decrease in GLUT1 transporters would slow down the process of glucose entering cells, and would also mean that there is less GLUT1 available to transport glucose from the blood to the cells.  Both of these effects would contribute to higher levels of glucose in the blood.  The decrease in lypolysis that occurs as a result of GH would actually decrease the amount of free fatty acids available to be converted into glucose, and so would actually work to decrease levels of glucose in the blood.  So, E is the wrong answer.  I hope this explanation helps. input: Given question: Calcinosis is the calcification of soft tissues ( including kidneys,heart , lungs etc) What vitamin could cause this if it is ingested in excess? Option A: A Option B: B6 Option C: B9 Option D: D The correct answer is Option D.
reference: Vitamin D, when ingested in excess can causecalcinosis. This can occur through a few different mechanisms. One is that it causes increased absorption of calcium, and so more calcium is laid down in soft tissues. Another is that it inhibits the function of 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferal (the activated from of vitamin D) which is responsible for promoting bone health and reducing calcium levels in the blood. This means that more calcium is released from bones and into the blood, where it can be deposited in soft tissues such as the kidneys and heart.  Too much vitamin A can also cause calcinosis, but this is far less common.  Too much vitamin D is most commonly encountered as a result of sun worshipping or using sunbeds.  Symptoms of vitamin D toxicity include; vomiting, diarrhoea, confusion, cardiac arrhythmias and in severe cases renal failure.  It is rare to get vitamin D toxicity through just dietary intake, however, it is possible if one were to consume large amounts of foods that are fortified with vitamin D (e.g. cereal, milk and orange juice), or if one takes a lot of supplements containing vitamin D.  It is important to note that many people do not ingest enough vitamin D, and so may develop rickets (a disease that affects bone development) as a result.  I hope this helps! input: Given question: You are well into your shift at the A&E department, You have requested a blood gas on one of the patients and the results show that their partial pressure of oxygen is less than 8KPa, but their partial pressure of carbon dioxide is normal. You suspected type 1 respiratory failure and began treatment with oxygen and go on your way. A few hours later you return to see that the oxygen treatment isnt working and the patient is showing no signs of improvement. What was the cause of his respiratory failure? Option A: Low PiO2 Option B: VQ mismatch Option C: Pulmonary shunt Option D: diffusion impairment Option E: hypoventilation. The correct answer is Option C.
reference: 8Kpa is equal to 80mmHg, this is the upper limit of normal for the partial pressure of oxygen in the blood. This patient has pulmonary shunt, where by the blood is bypassing the alveoli and going straight to the pulmonary capillaries so the oxygen dissociates from the haemoglobin and goes into the blood stream, however since there is no ventilation the CO2 levels remain high causing type 1 respiratory failure. In this instance oxygen treatment would not work as the root cause of the problem is lack of ventilation, not low oxygen levels. To treat this you would need to intubate the patient and ventilate them artificially.
best_explanation: If theres a pulmonary shunt, theres an uncoupling of the O2 transport from the ventilation. The cause of this can be an increase in the A-a gradient, this causes the O2 dissociation curve to shift to the right, meaning that even though theres more O2 in the alveoli, it is not able to diffuse into the blood. Another cause is an increase in the resistance in the alveoli and/or the capillaries, this reduces the net diffusion pressure.  In type 1 respiratory failure you would expect that the paO2 would be low, but in this case there is no change in paO2, so its not type 1, but there still is failure, so its type 2.  In type 2 respiratory failure, theres an increase in the A-a gradient, and so the oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right. this means that even though theres more O2 in the alveoli, it cant diffuse into the blood, so theres no change in paO2.  in type 1, you would expect that the paO2 would be low and there would be no change in paCO2, but in type 2, theres no change in paO2 and paCO2 rises.  in type 2, you would treat with high flow oxygen, and in type 1, you would treat with the highest flow of oxygen possible and the patient would be intubated.  Another way of remembering the difference is that in type 1, theres an issue with the blood, in type 2, theres an issue with the alveoli.  In this case, the answer is C, pulmonary shunt.  A, D and B are all causes of type 1 respiratory failure, and E is a cause of hypoventilation.  Pulmonary shunt can be caused by an increase in the A-a gradient, this can be caused by: increased resistance in the alveoli and/or capillaries, increased ventilation-perfusion ratio, and bronchoconstriction.  You would treat this by trying to reduce the A-a gradient, this can be done by: decreasing the resistance, increasing the ventilation-perfusion ratio, and treating the underlying cause of bronchoconstriction. reference:
​The kidneys are covered in visceral peritoneum but also contain a layer of loose connective tissue called the parietal peritoneum. This means they are only partially intraperitoneal. The other answer that would be partially correct is the appendix which is also partially covered by parietal peritoneum. https://teachmeanatomy.info/abdomen/cavities-and-ligaments/intraperitoneal-visceral/ - has good explanations and diagrams on intraperitoneal visceral organs and partial cover of parietal peritoneum. https://www.histology.leeds.ac.uk/digestive/kidney/kidney_1.php - has good info on kidney histology including layers of peritoneum. https://teachmeanatomy.info/abdomen/cavities-and-ligaments/parietal-peritoneal/ - explains parietal peritoneum and its function. https://www.histology.leeds.ac.uk/digestive/appendix/appendix_1.php - has information on appendix histology including layers of peritoneum. https://www.histology.leeds.ac.uk/digestive/stomach/stomach_1.php - has information on stomach histology including layers of peritoneum. https://www.histology.leeds.ac.uk/digestive/liver/liver_1.php - has information on liver histology including layers of peritoneum. http://www.anatomystuff.co.uk/encyclopaedia/C/Intraperitoneal+Visceral+Organs.htm - good summary of intraperitoneal visceral organs and their peritoneal covering.

best_explanation: The kidneys are covered in visceral peritoneum but also contain a layer of loose connective tissue (subperitoneal layer) between the visceral peritoneum and the kidney itself. This allows them to be located slightly more freely within the abdominal cavity, and for them to be able to be moved slightly in response to changes in position of the diaphragm (kidney mobility).  The other organs listed are all classed as intraperitoneal.  For the appendix, this is a straight forward question. For the transverse colon, remember that the peritoneum also lines the outside of the colon (subperitoneal).  Refer to Jittima's introduction to the abdomen plenary for more detail.  PCS Unit 2 Little bit of history - The peritoneum was once thought to be a closed cavity, but we now know that it is a series of small cavities separated by strands of peritoneum. (See PCS unit 2 tissue session 7) Importance - The peritoneum is a potential space in which bodily fluids (such as blood and lymph) can be efficiently drained away to be processed by other organs. It also allows for the easy movement of organs within the abdominal cavity. Peritonitis is the inflammation of the peritoneum - usually occurs as a complication of appendicitis, perforated ulcer or a ruptured ovarian cyst. Symptoms: fever, muscle wasting, weakness, abdominal pain. Treatment: usually involves removing the source of infection and giving antibiotics. Complications: can cause sepsis and ultimately death if untreated.  Sources: PCS unit 2 tissue session 7 document (led by Prof. Wilson) and Jittima's introduction to the abdomen plenary. input: Given question: Your driving down the M4 when you look in your mirror and and see someone is right up behind you, too close for comfort. reference:
100-120 compression per minute (this allows for adequate blood flow whilst not causing too much muscle fatigue for the rescuer) press down 5-6cm (this allows for adequate blood flow to the brain without causing any damage to the heart or other organs) remember its 30:2 for children under 10kg and for adults if they are obese or have a GCS score under 6 then its 30:2 instead of 16:2. Also make sure to check for responsiveness every 30 secs. If there is any change in response then stop and reassess. Remember that CPR is a basic life support procedure that can be learnt by anyone. Its not perfect but its better than nothing. Hopefully you will never need to use it but if you do remember that the person performing CPR is doing their best and is acting in good faith. The information used in this scenario is based on the Resuscitation Council (UK) guidelines for CPR. https://www.resus.org.uk/pages/start-cpraed.aspx https://www.resus.org.uk/pages/outcomeaftercardiacarrest.aspx The case 2 lecture 'first aid and emergencies' may also be useful. The scenario did not state whether any other people were present or if the phone was nearby to call for help. Remember if you are alone with the casualty you should only perform 1 cycle of CPR (30 secs) before going to get help. If you are with someone else you should perform 2 cycles of CPR before going for help. Also remember if you are unable to perform CPR due to fear or any other reason you should stand clear of the casualty and shout for help. If you are unable to perform CPR for any reason then you must tell the paramedics when they arrive. They will take over from you and will be able to assist with CPR. It acts as a bridge for neutrophils to cross the endothelium. Fibrin is a protein involved in the platelet plug formation. It is laid down by the platelets after they have come to rest on the subendothelial surface. Keratin is a structural protein found in the cytoskeleton of mammalian epithelial cells. It is not involved in neutrophil migration. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: You are shadowing an eye surgeon and he suddenly turns to you and asks, 'WHAT TYPE OF COLLAGEN IS FOUND IN THE CORNEA!!!!'. You are caught off-guard and can't quite remember what type. What type of collagen is found in the cornea? Option A: Type I Option B: Type II Option C: Type III Option D: Type IV Option E: Type V The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
The cornea is made up of Type I collagen. This is the same as scar tissue and bone. It is a structural collagen. There are 3 main layers to the cornea - epithelium, Bowman's membrane (Type IV collagen) and stroma (Type I collagen). The stroma is the thickest layer and is made almost entirely of Type I collagen. This gives the cornea it's strength. In addition, there are also nerve endings, blood vessels and macrophages present in the stroma. The cornea has a very high oxygen concentration which is important in preventing infection by reducing the numbers of microorganisms that can survive. The cornea also contains some keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate. These give the cornea additional strength and help to prevent dehydration. The epithelium is composed of multiple layers of cells which are held together by desmosine and laminine. The most important cell in the epithelium is the corneal keratocyte. It is believed that these cells are responsible for creating new corneas in case of damage. Finally, the Bowman's membrane is a thin layer of collagen that separates the cornea from the sclera. It is named after its discoverer, Sir William Bowman. It is thought that this layer may help to even out any irregularities in the surface of the cornea so that the light is not distorted as it enters the eye. If there is damage to the cornea, the body produces new collagen for the Bowman's membrane to repair it.  Adapted from PCS Unit 1 - The Cornea and Conjunctiva lecture.
=================================================================================================================================================== For more information refer to - https://www.ucl.ac.uk/postgraduate-medicine/eyes/cornea/structure https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441980/#:~:text=The%20stroma%20is%20the%20thickest,endothelial%20cells%20in%20the%20iris.&text=The%20epithelium%20is%20composed,layers%20of%20cells%20are%20held%20together.&text=The%20Bowman%27s%20membrane%20is,surface%20of%20the%20cornea%20is%20not%20distorted.&text=Finally%2C%20the%20Bowman%27s%20membrane,the%20body%20produces%20new%20collagen%20for%20repair.&sort=asc#FN1-6E5D8F9F161728C (this link takes you to the structure of the cornea page on LC, but it is under construction at the moment so I cannot direct you to a specific page) Please note that there is an awful lot of information here so if you have any questions or need clarification on anything please don't hesitate to ask! I hope you find this helpful :)  Disclaimer: I am not a medical professional so this information should not be used to diagnose or treat any conditions. It is just general knowledge that I have learnt and wanted to share :)
best_explanation: The cornea is made up of type I collagen. This is the same collagen found in bone. The cornea has a high amount of type I collagen which gives it strength and rigidity. This is important as the cornea is constantly under pressure from the eyelids and eyelashes when the eye blinks. Type I collagen is also found in the sclera which is the white part of the eye. The lens is made up of type II collagen. This type of collagen is found in the dermis and is also found in the cartilage. It gives the lens its flexibility. The vitreous humour is made up of type III collagen. This type of collagen is found in the skin and is also found in the scar tissue. It gives the vitreous humour its jell like consistency. The retina is made up of type IV collagen. This type of collagen is found in the blood vessels and is also found in the basal lamina. It helps the retina to stick to the back of the eye. The optic nerve is made up of type V collagen. This type of collagen is found in the bone and is also found in the cartilage.  P.S - there is no type VI collagen. This was a trick question. If you are unsure what type of collagen is found in the cornea, you can always just look it up. I didn't actually shadow an eye surgeon and I just looked this up. I hope this was helpful and you now know what type of collagen is found in the cornea. If you have any questions feel free to ask. I'm here to help. :)

input: Given question: Which of the following imaging methods does not use ionising radiation? Option A: CT scan Option B: Fluoroscopy Option C: MRI Option D: PET scan Option E: X-rays The correct answer is Option C.
reference: CT scans - uses ionising radiation (X-rays) to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs. They are often used to diagnose problems such as tumours, cysts, fractures and infections.  Fluoroscopy - uses ionising radiation (X-rays) to produce real-time moving images of the inside of the body. It is often used to guide procedures such as injections or biopsies.  PET scans - also uses ionising radiation (positron emission tomography) to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs. However, they work by detecting the gamma rays emitted by a tracer substance (such as glucose) rather than by exposure to X-rays directly.  X-rays - non-invasive diagnostic test that uses ionising radiation to produce images of the body's tissues and organs. They are commonly used to diagnose conditions of the bones, joints, heart, lungs and digestive system.  MRI - does not expose the body to ionising radiation. Instead, it uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to produce detailed images of the body's tissues and organs.  Ultrasound - also does not expose the body to ionising radiation. Instead, it uses high frequency sound waves to produce images of the body's tissues and organs. It is commonly used during pregnancy to check on the development of the foetus. This was taken from 'Imaging techniques overview' on the Cancer Research UK website.  I hope this helps! Let me know if you have any questions. Fluoroscopy - uses ionising radiation (X-rays) to produce real-time moving images. It is often used to guide procedures such as injections or biopsies.  MRI - does not use ionising radiation. It produces detailed images of the body's soft tissues such as muscles and organs. Some may be able to develop into blastocysts but most will be absorbed by the endometrium. input: Given question: Mr. Mann comes in to see you at your GP practice. He presents with numbness in the thenar eminence of his palm in addition to pain and tingling in his thumb and lateral two and a half fingers. You diagnose him with: Option A: Klumpke Paralysis Option B: Erb-Duchenne Palsy Option C: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Option D: Claw Hand The correct answer is Option C.
reference: https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/nerves/median-nerve/carpal-tunnel/ - clinical relevance box at bottomCarpal tunnel syndrome occurs when there is entrapment of the median nerve as it travels through the wrist at the carpal tunnel. This causes pain, numbness and tingling in the hand. It can be caused by anything that reduces the size of the carpal tunnel (eg oedema). In this case, the thenar eminence (located on the anterior surface of the palm) is also affected because the median nerve supplies the flexors of the hand (including the flexor pollicis longus which flexes the thumb at the MCP joint). Therefore, weakness of the thenar eminence (ie poor grip) is common. There are several ways to treat carpal tunnel syndrome (non-surgical and surgical) but the most important thing is to identify and address any underlying cause (eg diabetes, obesity). best_explanation: The thenar eminence is innervated by the median nerve. In this case, the numbness in the thenar eminence suggests damage to the median nerve. The pain and tingling in the thumb and lateral 2.5 fingers is commonly referred to as "Gilliatt-Sumner hand" and is also a result of damage to the median nerve.  Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the median nerve as it travels through the wrist at the carpal tunnel. The median nerve innervates the thenar eminence and the thumb, index finger and middle finger.  Erb-Duchenne palsy is a paralysis of the arm caused by damage to the upper group of the arm's main nerves, specifically the severing of the upper trunk C5-C6 nerves. This would not be caused by carpal tunnel syndrome.  Klumpke paralysis is a paralysis of the arm caused by damage to the lower group of the arm's main nerves, specifically the severing of the lower trunk C5-C7 nerves.
